title: Fire eats obstacles
hookLine: the mind turns obstacles into fuel, like fire burning what's thrown on it (Meditations 4.1)

lines: THE SAME LOG ON A CAMPFIRE.
cards: Drop a damp log on a candle and the candle goes out. Drop the same log on a roaring campfire and it hisses, smokes for a moment, then catches, and the fire stands taller than before. Same log.
Different fire. Marcus Aurelius opens his fourth book with that picture, a little lamp and a bright fire side by side. It's about what happens when plans run into a wall.

teach.h: THE MIND ADAPTS TO WHAT'S GIVEN.
teach.b: When the mind that governs us is in line with nature, Marcus writes, it meets whatever happens by adjusting easily to what's possible and what's given. It doesn't demand one particular material to work with.

It moves toward its aims, but with a reservation. That's a Stoic idea: you aim, and you hold the aim lightly, with an unspoken if nothing prevents me. If something does prevent you, you haven't failed at what mattered.
And whatever comes against it, the mind makes into material for itself, like a fire seizing what falls on it. A small lamp would be put out.

A bright fire takes in whatever is heaped on it, eats it up, and rises higher because of it. Notice what Marcus is not saying. He isn't saying obstacles are secretly good, or that every setback is a blessing in disguise.

He's saying the obstacle can become fuel for the person you're actually trying to be. Your flight is canceled: material for patience. A coworker takes credit: material for fairness, and for speaking up well.
Your plan dies: material for courage. For a Stoic, the plan was never the whole point. The kind of person you are while planning was the point, and an obstacle can't take that away.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius recall the fire image of Meditations 4.1 when plans fail, asking what quality the obstacle could become material for.

o: the emperor who said the mind turns obstacles into fuel
a Roman general who burned his enemies' supplies
a Greek poet who wrote that every setback is a blessing

s: Marcus says every setback is a blessing in disguise
he says the obstacle can become material for virtue, not that it's secretly good.
the fire image opens the fourth book of the Meditations
4.1: a bright fire takes in what's heaped on it and rises higher.
the Stoic 'reservation' means aiming while holding the aim lightly
you aim, with an unspoken 'if nothing prevents me'.

games.q: the job you worked months for goes to someone else. what fits Meditations 4.1?
o: ask what this loss could be material for.
games.why: Marcus says the mind makes whatever opposes it into material, as fire takes in what falls on it and rises higher.

practice: Bring to mind one obstacle in your way right now, a delay, a person, a no, and picture it as a log landing on your fire, hissing and smoking for a moment.
Then ask what it could be material for: patience, honesty, kindness, a new way around. Pick one, and picture the fire catching and standing taller.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who pictured a mind in line with nature turning whatever blocks it into material, the way a bright fire burns what's thrown on it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'fire': the image Marcus uses in 4.1 for a mind that feeds on obstacles.
